stem: Which of the following best describes the position of the parietal lobe:
options: Anterior to the central sulcus and superior to the lateral sulcus
Posterior to the central sulcus and superior to the lateral sulcus
Anterior to the central sulcus and inferior to the lateral sulcus
Posterior to the central sulcus and inferior to the lateral sulcus
fact: The parietal lobe lies posterior to the central sulcus and superior to the lateral sulcus, extending posteriorly toward the occipital lobe.
mnemonic: Parietal is posterior to central and perched above lateral.
finding: The reference states that the parietal lobe is posterior to the central sulcus and anterior to the parieto-occipital sulcus; the lateral fissure separates the temporal lobe from frontal and parietal lobes.

stem: The blood supply to the frontal lobe is primarily supplied by which of the following arteries:
fact: The frontal lobe receives anterior cerebral artery supply on its medial surface and middle cerebral artery supply on its lateral surface.
mnemonic: Frontal has two main friends: ACA medial, MCA lateral.
finding: The cortex reference describes the anterior cerebral artery supply to the anteromedial hemisphere and middle cerebral artery supply to the lateral surface, including frontal motor regions.

stem: The sensation produced by touching the arm with cotton wool during a neurological examination is mediated by which of the following spinal tracts:
fact: Fine touch is carried in the posterior-column–medial-lemniscus pathway; the posterior columns also carry vibration and proprioception.
mnemonic: DCML = Discriminative touch, Conscious proprioception, vibration, Medial Lemniscus.
finding: The posterior-column reference identifies the dorsal column pathway as carrying fine touch, vibration, and proprioception.

stem: A 69 year old patient is brought to ED with acute onset facial weakness on the right side, and difficulty with speech. He is able to respond to questions appropriately by nodding or shaking his head, but his words are jumbled and don't make sense. Which of the following lobes has been affected:
fact: A dominant left frontal-lobe lesion can affect the primary motor cortex, causing right facial weakness, and Broca area, causing expressive dysphasia.
mnemonic: Left frontal: face moves right, Broca makes speech.
finding: The reference locates the primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe and Broca area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, supporting the displayed left-frontal localization.

stem: Which of the following best describes the position of the occipital lobe:
options: Posterior to the central sulcus and inferior to the lateral sulcus
Posterior to the central sulcus and superior to the lateral sulcus
fact: The occipital lobe lies posterior to the parieto-occipital sulcus and rests inferiorly on the tentorium cerebelli.
mnemonic: Occipital is the back-and-bottom lobe: posterior and inferior.
finding: The reference places the occipital lobe posterior to the parieto-occipital sulcus and superior to the tentorium cerebelli.

stem: A 49 year old presents to ED complaining of muscle weakness and clumsiness in the right hand, with slow and effortful speech. In which of the following lobes is the lesion most likely found:
fact: Right-hand motor impairment and slow, effortful expressive speech point to the dominant left frontal lobe, involving motor and Broca regions.
mnemonic: Dominant frontal = force plus fluent production problem; right hand points left.
finding: The precentral-gyrus reference locates primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus; the cerebral-hemisphere reference locates Broca area in the dominant frontal lobe.

stem: Which of the following clinical features is most suggestive of a lesion of the parietal lobe:
fact: Hemispatial neglect is a classic clinical association of nondominant parietal-lobe dysfunction, especially on the right.
mnemonic: Parietal neglects a half: space and sensation are missed.
finding: The cerebral-hemisphere reference describes nondominant parietal damage as producing contralateral hemispatial neglect.

stem: What type of visual field defect are you most likely to see in a lesion at the optic chiasm:
fact: An optic-chiasm lesion disrupts the crossing nasal retinal fibres and causes loss of the temporal visual fields of both eyes, producing bitemporal hemianopia.
mnemonic: Chiasm crossing cuts the outer fields: bitemporal loss.
finding: The reference states that lesions impinging on the optic chiasm commonly result in bitemporal hemianopsia by affecting decussating nasal fibres.

stem: A 68 year old lady was involved in a road traffic accident and describes a whiplash type injury. She has pain and tenderness in the cervical region and imaging shows a herniated disc in this region. The patient is complaining of weakness of elbow extension and loss of sensation over the middle finger. Which of the following spinal nerves is most likely affected:
fact: The C7 root is associated with elbow extension and sensation in the middle-finger distribution, making C7 the best answer for this cervical radiculopathy pattern.
mnemonic: C7 = straighten the elbow and sense the middle finger.
sourceLabel: NCBI Bookshelf spinal-cord and root anatomy
finding: The source page displays C7; its clinical explanation links C7 to elbow extension and middle-finger sensation.

stem: CSF is reabsorbed from subarachnoid space via which of the following structures:
fact: Arachnoid granulations project into the dural venous sinuses and provide the principal route for CSF reabsorption from the subarachnoid space.
mnemonic: Granulations drain CSF into venous circulation.
finding: The displayed explanation identifies arachnoid granulations protruding into dural venous sinuses as the route from subarachnoid CSF back to circulation.
